question: What are the three key concerns for most software systems, and what does the first one mean?
source_chunk_text: In this book, we focus on three concerns that are important in most software systems: Reliability The system should continue to work correctly (performing the correct function at the desired performance) even in the face of adversity (hardware or software faults, and even human error).
ideal_answer: The three concerns are reliability, scalability, and maintainability. Reliability means the system should continue to work correctly — performing the correct function at the desired performance — even in the face of adversity such as hardware or software faults and human error.

question: What is the difference between a fault and a failure in a system?
source_chunk_text: Note that a fault is not the same as a failure [2]. A fault is usually defined as one com! ponent of the system deviating from its spec, whereas a failure is when the system as a whole stops providing the required service to the user. It is impossible to reduce the probability of a fault to zero; therefore it is usually best to design fault tolerance mechanisms that prevent faults from causing failures.
ideal_answer: A fault is one component of the system deviating from its spec, whereas a failure is when the system as a whole stops providing the required service to the user. Since faults cannot be reduced to zero probability, it is best to design fault-tolerance mechanisms that prevent faults from causing failures.

question: Given typical hard disk failure rates, how often should a disk death be expected on a storage cluster with 10,000 disks?
source_chunk_text: Hard disks crash, RAM becomes faulty, the power grid has a blackout, someone unplugs the wrong network cable. Anyone who has worked with large data centers can tell you that these things happen all the time when you have a lot of machines. Hard disks are reported as having a mean time to failure (MTTF) of about 10 to 50 years [5, 6]. Thus, on a storage cluster with 10,000 disks, we should expect on average one disk to die per day.
ideal_answer: On average one disk should be expected to die per day. This follows from hard disks having a reported mean time to failure (MTTF) of about 10 to 50 years.

question: What happens to software projects as they grow larger, and what is a project mired in complexity sometimes called?
source_chunk_text: Small software projects can have delightfully simple and expressive code, but as projects get larger, they often become very complex and difficult to understand. This complexity slows down everyone who needs to work on the system, further increas! ing the cost of maintenance. A software project mired in complexity is sometimes described as a big ball of mud [30].
ideal_answer: As projects grow larger they often become very complex and difficult to understand, which slows down everyone working on the system and increases maintenance cost. A software project mired in complexity is sometimes described as a big ball of mud.

question: What is one of the best tools for removing accidental complexity in software, and what does it do?
source_chunk_text: One of the best tools we have for removing accidental complexity is abstraction. A good abstraction can hide a great deal of implementation detail behind a clean, simple-to-understand façade. A good abstraction can also be used for a wide range of different applications. Not only is this reuse more efficient than re-implementing a similar thing multiple times, but it also leads to higher-quality software, as quality improvements in the abstracted component benefit all applications that use it.
ideal_answer: Abstraction is one of the best tools for removing accidental complexity. A good abstraction hides implementation detail behind a clean, simple-to-understand façade, can be reused across many applications, and leads to higher-quality software because improvements in the abstracted component benefit all applications that use it.

question: Who proposed the relational model and how does it organize data?
source_chunk_text: The best-known data model today is probably that of SQL, based on the relational model proposed by Edgar Codd in 1970 [1]: data is organized into relations (in SQL: tables), where each relation is an unordered collection of tuples (rows).
ideal_answer: The relational model was proposed by Edgar Codd in 1970. It organizes data into relations (called tables in SQL), where each relation is an unordered collection of tuples (rows).

question: Where did the term NoSQL originally come from?
source_chunk_text: Now, in the 2010s, NoSQL is the latest attempt to overthrow the relational model’s dominance. The term NoSQL is unfortunate, since it doesn’t actually refer to any par! ticular technology — it was intended simply as a catchy Twitter hashtag for a meetup on open source, distributed, non-relational databases in 2009 [3].
ideal_answer: The term NoSQL does not refer to any particular technology — it was originally intended as a catchy Twitter hashtag for a 2009 meetup on open source, distributed, non-relational databases.

question: How were records linked and accessed in the network model?
source_chunk_text: The links between records in the network model are not foreign keys, but more like pointers in a programming language (while still being stored on disk). The only way of accessing a record was to follow a path from a root record along these chains of links. This was called an access path.
ideal_answer: In the network model, links between records were not foreign keys but more like pointers in a programming language stored on disk. The only way to access a record was to follow a path from a root record along these chains of links, which was called an access path.

question: Why is it misleading to call document databases schemaless?
source_chunk_text: Document databases are sometimes called schemaless, but that’s misleading, as the code that reads the data usually assumes some kind of structure  — i.e. there is an implicit schema, but it is not enforced by the database [20].
ideal_answer: Calling document databases schemaless is misleading because the code that reads the data usually assumes some kind of structure — there is an implicit schema, it is just not enforced by the database.

question: What components make up a vertex in the property graph model?
source_chunk_text: In the property graph model, each vertex consists of: •a unique identifier, •a set of outgoing edges, •a set of incoming edges, and •a collection of properties (key-value pairs).
ideal_answer: In the property graph model, each vertex consists of a unique identifier, a set of outgoing edges, a set of incoming edges, and a collection of properties as key-value pairs.

question: How is information stored in a triple-store?
source_chunk_text: In a triple-store, all information is stored in the form of very simple three-part state! ments: (subject, predicate, object). For example, in the triple (Jim, likes, bananas), Jim is the subject, likes is the predicate (verb), and bananas is the object.
ideal_answer: In a triple-store, all information is stored as simple three-part statements of the form (subject, predicate, object). For example, in the triple (Jim, likes, bananas), Jim is the subject, likes is the predicate, and bananas is the object.

question: What is the general idea behind a database index?
source_chunk_text: In order to efficiently find the value for a particular key in the database, we need a different data structure: an index. In this chapter we will look at a range of indexing structures and see how they compare. But the general idea behind them is: keep some additional metadata on the side, which acts as a signpost and helps you to locate the data you want.
ideal_answer: An index is a data structure needed to efficiently find the value for a particular key in a database. The general idea is to keep additional metadata on the side, which acts as a signpost and helps locate the data you want.

question: What is the fundamental trade-off when adding indexes to a database?
source_chunk_text: This is an important trade-off in storage systems: well-chosen indexes speed up read queries, but every index slows down writes. For this reason, databases don’t usually index everything by default, but require you — the application developer or database administrator — to choose indexes manually, using your knowledge of the applica! tion’s typical query patterns.
ideal_answer: Well-chosen indexes speed up read queries, but every index slows down writes. That is why databases do not index everything by default and instead require the developer or database administrator to choose indexes manually based on the application's typical query patterns.

question: What does compaction mean in a log-structured storage engine, and why is it needed?
source_chunk_text: As described so far, we only ever append to a file — so how do we avoid eventually running out of disk space? A good solution is to break the log into segments of a cer! tain size, and to perform compaction on these segments, as illustrated in Figure 3-2. Compaction means throwing away duplicate keys in the log, and keeping only the most recent update for each key.
ideal_answer: Compaction means throwing away duplicate keys in the log and keeping only the most recent update for each key. It is needed because an append-only log would otherwise eventually run out of disk space, so the log is broken into segments of a certain size and compaction is performed on them.

question: What happens when a new key does not fit into a B-tree page, and what height does a B-tree with n keys have?
source_chunk_text: If there isn’t enough free space in the page to accommodate the new key, it is split into two half-full pages, and the parent page is updated to account for the new subdi! vision of key ranges — see Figure 3-7.iii This algorithm ensures that the tree remains balanced: a B-tree with n keys always has a height of O(log n). Even if the tree is very large, you don’t need to follow many page references to find the page you are looking for.
ideal_answer: If there is not enough free space in the page for the new key, the page is split into two half-full pages and the parent page is updated to reflect the new subdivision of key ranges. This keeps the tree balanced, so a B-tree with n keys always has a height of O(log n).

question: What is a write-ahead log and why do B-tree implementations use one?
source_chunk_text: In order to make the database resilient to crashes, it is normal for B-tree implementa! tions to include an additional data structure on disk: a write-ahead log (WAL, also known as redo log). This is an append-only file to which every B-tree modification must be written before it can be applied to the pages of the tree itself. When the data! base comes back up after a crash, this log is used to restore the B-tree back to a con! sistent state [5, 19].
ideal_answer: A write-ahead log (WAL, also known as redo log) is an append-only file to which every B-tree modification must be written before it is applied to the pages of the tree itself. B-tree implementations use it to make the database resilient to crashes: after a crash, the log is used to restore the B-tree to a consistent state.

question: Why can LSM-trees typically sustain higher throughput of random writes than B-trees?
source_chunk_text: LSM-trees are typically able to sustain much higher throughput of random writes compared to B-trees, because they turn all random writes into sequential writes on the underlying device. This makes them appealing for applications with high write throughput. As a rule of thumb, LSM-trees are typically faster for writes, whereas B- trees are thought to be faster for reads [22].
ideal_answer: LSM-trees turn all random writes into sequential writes on the underlying device, which lets them sustain much higher random write throughput than B-trees. As a rule of thumb, LSM-trees are typically faster for writes while B-trees are thought to be faster for reads.

question: What is a covering index?
source_chunk_text: A compromise between a clustered index (storing all row data within the index) and a nonclustered index (storing only references to the data within the index) is known as a covering index or index with included columns, which stores some of a table’s col! umns within the index [27]. This allows some queries to be answered by using the index alone (in which case, the index is said to cover the query) [26].
ideal_answer: A covering index (or index with included columns) is a compromise between a clustered index and a nonclustered index: it stores some of a table's columns within the index. This allows some queries to be answered by using the index alone, in which case the index is said to cover the query.

question: How does sorted order help with compression in column-oriented storage?
source_chunk_text: Another advantage of sorted order is that it can help with compression of columns. If the primary sort column does not have many distinct values, then after sorting, it will have long sequences where the same value is repeated many times in a row. A simple run-length encoding, like we used for the bitmaps in Figure 3-11, could compress that column down to a few kilobytes — even if the table has billions of rows.
ideal_answer: If the primary sort column does not have many distinct values, sorting produces long sequences where the same value is repeated many times in a row. A simple run-length encoding can then compress that column down to a few kilobytes even if the table has billions of rows.

question: In Avro, do the writer's schema and the reader's schema have to be identical?
source_chunk_text: The key idea with Avro is that the writer’s schema and the reader’s schema don’t have to be the same — they only need to be compatible. When data is decoded (read), the Avro library resolves the differences by looking at the writer’s schema and the reader’s schema side-by-side, and translating the data from the writer’s schema into the reader’s schema.
ideal_answer: No. The key idea with Avro is that the writer's schema and the reader's schema only need to be compatible, not identical. When data is decoded, the Avro library resolves the differences by looking at both schemas side-by-side and translating the data from the writer's schema into the reader's schema.

question: What rule must be followed in Avro to maintain schema compatibility when adding or removing fields?
source_chunk_text: To maintain compatibility, you may only add or remove a field that has a default value. (The field favoriteNumber in the Avro schema above has a default value of null.) For example, say you add a field with a default value, so this new field exists in the new schema but not the old one. When a reader using the new schema reads a record written with the old schema, the default value is filled in for the missing field.
ideal_answer: To maintain compatibility in Avro, you may only add or remove a field that has a default value. When a reader using the new schema reads a record written with the old schema, the default value is filled in for the missing field.

question: What is REST and what does it emphasize?
source_chunk_text: REST is not a protocol, but rather a design philosophy that builds upon the principles of HTTP [33, 34]. It emphasizes simple data formats, using URLs for identifying resources, and using HTTP features for cache control, authentication, and content type negotiation. REST has been gaining popularity compared to SOAP, at least in the context of cross-organizational service integration [35] and is often associated with microservices [31].
ideal_answer: REST is not a protocol but a design philosophy that builds upon the principles of HTTP. It emphasizes simple data formats, using URLs to identify resources, and using HTTP features for cache control, authentication, and content type negotiation, and it has been gaining popularity compared to SOAP.

question: How does a network request differ from a local function call in terms of predictability?
source_chunk_text: •A local function call is predictable, and either succeeds or fails, depending only on parameters that are under your control. A network request is unpredictable: the request or response may be lost due to a network problem, or the remote machine may be slow or unavailable, and such problems are entirely outside of your control. Network problems are common, so you have to anticipate them, for example by retrying a failed request.
ideal_answer: A local function call is predictable and either succeeds or fails depending only on parameters under your control. A network request is unpredictable: the request or response may be lost due to a network problem, or the remote machine may be slow or unavailable — problems entirely outside your control that must be anticipated, for example by retrying failed requests.

question: In a shared-nothing architecture, what is a node and how do nodes coordinate with each other?
source_chunk_text: In this approach, each machine or virtual machine running the database software is called a node. Each node uses its CPUs, RAM and disks independently. Any coordination between nodes is done at the soft! ware level, using a conventional network. No special hardware is required by a shared-nothing system, so you can use whatever machines have the best price/performance ratio.
ideal_answer: A node is each machine or virtual machine running the database software, and each node uses its CPUs, RAM, and disks independently. Any coordination between nodes is done at the software level using a conventional network, so no special hardware is required.

question: What is the difference between replication and partitioning as ways of distributing data?
source_chunk_text: Replication Keeping a copy of the same data on several different nodes, potentially in differ! ent locations. Replication provides redundancy: if some nodes are unavailable, the data can still be served from the remaining nodes. Replication can also help improve performance. We discuss replication in Chapter 5. Partitioning Splitting a big database into smaller subsets called partitions, so that different partitions can be assigned to different nodes (also known as sharding). We dis! cuss partitioning in Chapter 6.
ideal_answer: Replication means keeping a copy of the same data on several different nodes, providing redundancy so data can still be served if some nodes are unavailable, and it can also improve performance. Partitioning (also known as sharding) means splitting a big database into smaller subsets called partitions so that different partitions can be assigned to different nodes.

question: Why is it impractical for all followers in a replicated database to be synchronous?
source_chunk_text: For that reason, it is impractical for all followers to be synchronous: any one node outage would cause the whole system to grind to a halt. In practice, if you enable syn! chronous replication on a database, it usually means that one of the followers is syn! chronous, and the others are asynchronous. If the synchronous follower becomes unavailable or goes slow, one of the asynchronous followers is made synchronous.
ideal_answer: If all followers were synchronous, any one node outage would cause the whole system to grind to a halt. In practice, enabling synchronous replication usually means one follower is synchronous and the others are asynchronous; if the synchronous follower becomes unavailable or slow, an asynchronous follower is made synchronous.

question: What steps are involved in failover when a database leader fails?
source_chunk_text: Handling a failure of the leader is trickier: one of the followers needs to be promoted to be the new leader, clients need to be reconfigured to send their writes to the new leader, and the other followers need to start consuming data changes from the new leader. This process is called failover.
ideal_answer: Failover involves promoting one of the followers to be the new leader, reconfiguring clients to send their writes to the new leader, and having the other followers start consuming data changes from the new leader.

question: What does read-after-write consistency guarantee, and what does it not promise?
source_chunk_text: In this situation, we need read-after-write consistency, also known as read-your-writes consistency [20]. This is a guarantee that if the user reloads the page, they will always see any updates they submitted themselves. It makes no promises about other users: other users’ updates may not be visible until some later time. However, it reassures the user that their own input has been saved correctly.
ideal_answer: Read-after-write consistency (also known as read-your-writes consistency) guarantees that if a user reloads the page, they will always see any updates they submitted themselves. It makes no promises about other users, whose updates may not be visible until some later time.

question: What guarantee do monotonic reads provide, and how does it compare to strong and eventual consistency?
source_chunk_text: Monotonic reads [19] is a guarantee that this kind of anomaly does not happen. It’s a lesser guarantee than strong consistency, but a stronger guarantee than eventual con! sistency. When you read data, you may see an old value; monotonic reads only means that if one user makes several reads in sequence, they will not see time go backwards, i.e. they will not read older data after having previously read newer data.
ideal_answer: Monotonic reads guarantee that if one user makes several reads in sequence, they will not see time go backwards — they will not read older data after having previously read newer data. It is a lesser guarantee than strong consistency but a stronger guarantee than eventual consistency.

question: How can two users editing the same wiki page at the same time cause a write conflict when each writes to a different leader?
source_chunk_text: For example, consider a wiki page that is simultaneously being edited by two users, as shown in Figure 5-7. User 1 changes the title of the page from A to B, and user 2 changes the title from A to C at the same time. Each user’s change is successfully applied to their local leader. However, when the changes are asynchronously replica! ted, a conflict is detected [28]. This problem does not occur in a single-leader data! base.
ideal_answer: If user 1 changes the page title from A to B while user 2 simultaneously changes it from A to C, each user's change is successfully applied to their local leader. When the changes are asynchronously replicated, a conflict is detected — a problem that does not occur in a single-leader database.
